faq.a: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. Because of this it is called a biological catalyst.
The active site is a small pocket on the enzyme with a special shape. Only a substrate with the matching shape can fit into it, which is why each enzyme does one job.
asks: Tell me about the substrate fitting
Why does each enzyme only do one job?

faq.a: Amylase breaks starch down into the sugar maltose. It is made in your salivary glands and pancreas.
asks: Why does bread taste sweet when chewed?

faq.a: No. After the products leave, the enzyme's active site is free again, so the same enzyme can be used over and over.

faq.q: What is the lock and key model?
faq.a: It is a way of picturing enzymes: the enzyme is the lock and the substrate is the key that fits it. A newer idea, the induced fit model, says the active site changes shape slightly to grip the substrate.

facts: Amylase in saliva begins breaking starch into maltose in the mouth.
Catalase can break down millions of hydrogen peroxide molecules per second.
